passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Miktam of David” (verse 1). Then a short prayer: “Preserve me, O God, for in You I take refuge” (verse 1).

He makes a confession of loyalty. “I said to the LORD, ‘You are my Lord; apart from You I have no good thing.’” (verse 2). His delight is in God's people, “the saints in the land” (verse 3). He will have nothing to do with “other gods” and their offerings (verse 4).

Then the heart of the psalm. “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure” (verse 5). “The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Miktam is a heading word whose meaning is not known. It also heads Psalms 56 to 60.

Verses 5 and 6 use the language of land. When Israel came into Canaan, the land was shared out among the tribes and families by lot (Joshua 14 to 19). The boundaries were marked with a measuring cord. A family's plot was its ‘inheritance’, passed down from parents to children. ‘The lines of my boundary’ are those measuring lines.

One tribe received no land. The priests and Levites had no plot, because God himself was their share. God told Aaron, “I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20). The psalmist takes that for himself. Others may have fields. He has God, and he calls it ‘delightful’.

Verse 4 speaks of ‘libations’, drink offerings poured out in worship. Its meaning in detail is uncertain, and Bibles translate verses 3 and 4 in different ways, because the Hebrew is short and hard.
passages.later:
Other believers in the Old Testament use the same words. “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26). In the middle of grief over a ruined city, Lamentations says, “‘The LORD is my portion,’ says my soul, ‘therefore I will hope in Him’” (Lamentations 3:24).

Jesus put first what verse 2 confesses: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37). Paul, writing from prison, says that knowing Christ is worth more than everything he lost (Philippians 3:8).
passages.hard:
‘Apart from You I have no good thing’ (verse 2). Does that mean nothing else in life is good: friends, work, food, beauty?

No. The next verse delights in God's people. Verse 6 enjoys a good inheritance. The Bible treats creation as good from its first page. The line means that God is the source and the best of every good thing. Nothing good stands apart from him, and nothing else could replace him.

There is a second question. Verse 4 speaks harshly of people who ‘chase other gods’. The psalmist does not attack them. He refuses to join them. That is the line he draws.
passages.asks:
What is your ‘portion’, the thing you count on to make life good? The psalm asks you to say honestly what you would most hate to lose.

Then try praying verse 5 as your own. Some days you will mean it fully. Some days it will be a prayer that you would come to mean it.

passages.t: ‘You will not abandon my soul to Sheol’, and the path of life
passages.happening:
The psalmist blesses God for guiding him, even at night. “I will bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my conscience instructs me” (verse 7).

“I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken” (verse 8). So his whole self is glad: heart, tongue and body. “Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely” (verse 9).

Then the line the apostles would preach. “For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (verse 10).

The psalm ends looking ahead: “You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
‘Conscience’ in verse 7 is in Hebrew ‘kidneys’. The kidneys stood for the deepest, hidden self. At night, in the quiet, God teaches him from the inside.

The ‘right hand’ was where a protector or helper stood. A defender in court stood at your right. Notice that the right hand appears twice: God is at the psalmist's right hand now (verse 8), and joy is at God's right hand forever (verse 11).

Sheol is the place of the dead (see the book page's part on Sheol). ‘Your Holy One’ translates a word built on hesed, God's faithful love: the one who belongs to God in loyal love.

‘Decay’ in verse 10 translates a Hebrew word that can mean ‘the pit’, the grave. Some modern Bibles put ‘the Pit’ there. The Greek translation of the Old Testament used a word for ‘corruption’ or ‘decay’, and the apostles quote it in that form. Either way the hope is the same: God will not leave his faithful one to death.
passages.later:
On the day of Pentecost, Peter quoted verses 8 to 11 (Acts 2:25-28). Then he argued from a simple fact: “the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day” (Acts 2:29). David's body did decay. So, Peter said, David “spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay” (Acts 2:31). (Hades is the Greek word for Sheol.) “God has raised this Jesus to life, to which we are all witnesses” (Acts 2:32).

Paul made the same argument in a synagogue in Pisidian Antioch. He quoted verse 10 and said that David “fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay” (Acts 13:36-37).

Paul also writes that “Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The ‘path of life’ of verse 11 opens for others through him.
passages.hard:
Did David know he was speaking of the resurrection, or did the apostles read that into his words later?

Christians answer in more than one way. Some scholars think David meant first that God would rescue him from an early death, and the apostles saw a fuller meaning after Easter. Others think verses 10 and 11 already reach past this life, with their talk of ‘the path of life’ and ‘eternal pleasures’, so that Peter was drawing out what was there. Many hold a view in between: David voiced a real hope that he could not fully see, and Jesus' rising made it plain. Peter himself calls David a prophet who saw it ahead of time (Acts 2:30-31).

All of these views agree on the main thing. The apostles did not use Psalm 16 to prove a vague hope. They used it to explain an event they had seen: a tomb in which the body did not stay.
passages.asks:
‘I have set the LORD always before me.’ The psalm asks you to practise that, on purpose, as a daily habit. Where does your mind turn first when you wake or when you are afraid?

It also asks you to face death with hope. For a Christian, the end of the road is not Sheol but ‘joy in Your presence’. If you are grieving someone who trusted Christ, verse 11 is a verse to hold.
